title: Taslima Nasrin Set to Return to Kolkata After 19 Years of Exile
excerpt: The exiled Bangladeshi author will attend a literary event at Rabindra Sadan on August 1, with West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari expected to share the stage in what organisers call a celebration of free speech.
body:
• Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin will visit Kolkata on August 1, her first return since being forced out in November 2007 during the Left Front government.
  • The literary event at Rabindra Sadan is organised by secular and anti-fundamentalist groups, with West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari expected to attend.
  • The BJP-led state government has framed the homecoming as a victory for free speech after previous Left Front and TMC administrations refused to facilitate Nasrin's return.
  • No discussion has taken place on whether the visit could lead to Nasrin's permanent resettlement in the city she has called her only home.

Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin is scheduled to return to Kolkata on August 1, nearly two decades after she was expelled from the city amid violent protests over her writings. Nasrin confirmed her participation in a literary event at Rabindra Sadan through a post on social media, ending years of uncertainty over whether she would ever set foot in the city again.

The event, organised by a coalition including Paschimbangar Jonno, Secular Mission, and the Human Rights and Basic Freedom Foundation, will feature cultural performances based on Nasrin's literary works, including recitations of her poetry and artistic presentations inspired by her writing. West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has been invited and is expected to attend, lending significant political weight to what organisers describe as a purely cultural occasion.

A Forced Departure That Shaped Bengal's Free Speech Debate

Nasrin was forced to leave Kolkata on November 21, 2007, after her book Dwikhondito triggered widespread unrest across several parts of the city. The situation deteriorated so rapidly that the administration called in the Army. The Left Front government under then-Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee banned the book and pressured Nasrin to leave, a decision widely criticised as capitulation to religious fundamentalist groups.

Born in what was then East Pakistan, Nasrin trained as a physician before turning to writing. She gained global attention in the early 1990s for her feminist critiques of organised religion and has lived in exile since 1994, with multiple fatwas calling for her death. After spending over a decade in Europe and the United States, she moved to India in 2004 and has remained on a resident permit visa.

"She was forced to leave Kolkata on 21 November 2007 after the then Left Front government bowed before fundamentalist forces. This is a new Bengal, and we have decided to honour her."

— Mohit Roy, Convenor, Paschimbangar Jonno

Political Symbolism Under a New Government

The timing of Nasrin's return is unmistakably political. The BJP assumed power in West Bengal after years of Trinamool Congress rule, and the party has seized on the homecoming as evidence that it stands for free expression where its predecessors did not.

"Successive Left Front and TMC governments chose political expediency over free speech by refusing to facilitate Taslima's return despite her repeated appeals to visit Kolkata for literary events and book fairs," said a senior BJP leader in West Bengal, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The issue gained fresh momentum last year when BJP Rajya Sabha MP Samik Bhattacharya, now the party's West Bengal president, urged the Indian government to facilitate Nasrin's return, calling her a "rare" voice who had consistently challenged fundamentalism. Organisers say there is no legal restriction on Nasrin's entry into the state — previous governments simply declined to provide the security guarantees needed for her visit.

The state government has now assured organisers of adequate security arrangements, with special measures expected to be in place for the duration of her stay.

A Homecoming, But Not Yet a Return

Despite the significance of the visit, organisers have been careful to manage expectations. Mohit Roy said no discussions have taken place about whether the August 1 event could pave the way for Nasrin's permanent return to the city.

Nasrin has repeatedly spoken about her deep emotional attachment to Kolkata, often describing it as her only true home after exile from Bangladesh. "I have no home other than Kolkata," she said in a previous interview. Although no formal prohibition prevented her from entering the city, a combination of security concerns and opposition from religious groups repeatedly disrupted earlier plans for public appearances.

Advocate Usman Malik, associated with the co-organising group Secular Mission, wrote on X that Nasrin's return to Kolkata after a long gap would be "a significant moment for freedom of expression and the fight against religious extremism."

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Nasrin's case has long been a touchstone in debates over free speech, secularism, and the political accommodation of religious conservatism in South Asia. Her forced departure from Kolkata in 2007 drew sharp criticism from writers and civil liberties groups worldwide. A successful visit — without incident — could signal a shift in how India's political establishment approaches dissenting voices, particularly those critical of religious orthodoxy.

The August 1 event at Rabindra Sadan will be closely watched not just in Kolkata but across the Bengali diaspora, for whom Nasrin remains a polarising yet defining literary figure. Whether the visit marks a symbolic gesture or the beginning of a more permanent homecoming remains an open question.
nri_angle: Nasrin's return tests India's commitment to free speech and secularism — issues that resonate deeply with the global Indian and Bengali diaspora.
